power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Prolonged military deployments expose personnel to sustained vigilance, disrupted sleep, uncertainty, repeated high-consequence decisions, separation from social support, and restricted opportunities for recovery.

Military organizations routinely monitor physical fitness and medical readiness, but stress-related neurocognitive functioning remains assessed primarily through self-report, observation, performance outcomes, and clinical contact.
These sources are indispensable, yet they may not reveal the physiological effort required to maintain performance or the capacity to recover after cognitive demand.
This paper introduces NPRO-8 MIL, a military adaptation of the NPRO-8 Core mental-fitness screening framework.
NPRO-8 MIL combines behavioral performance with functional near-infrared spectroscopy during five structured cognitive task modules.
Eight NeuroProbes inform three higher-order pillars: Stress Load, Recovery Capacity, and Functional Impact.

The underlying NPRO-8 Core has completed internal validation through 178 deterministic tests, 32,000 Monte Carlo examinations, 50,850 repeated robustness classifications, and parameter-sensitivity analyses.
These findings establish computational coherence and predictable behavior, while prospective military reliability, external-validity, and predictive-validity studies remain necessary.

Because fNIRS cannot feasibly be administered to every member of a large military population, a two-tier pathway is proposed: brief population-level digital screening followed by targeted NPRO-8 MIL assessment.
Ethical safeguards addressing voluntariness, privacy, command access, purpose limitation, and protection from unauthorized selection or disciplinary use are integral to the framework.
NPRO-8 MIL is presented as a screening and longitudinal monitoring approach, not a psychiatric diagnostic or autonomous fitness-for-duty instrument.
Military readiness depends on people sustaining effective performance under conditions that are deliberately demanding.

Prolonged deployments can combine extended duty hours, disrupted sleep and circadian rhythms, sustained vigilance, environmental constraint, uncertainty, separation from family and social support, and repeated exposure to high-consequence decisions.
These demands do not imply that every deployed service member will develop a mental-health condition.
They do create a setting in which load can accumulate, opportunities for recovery can narrow, and previously manageable demands can become progressively more difficult to regulate.
Fatigue is already recognized as a readiness concern in naval operations.

The U.S. Government Accountability Office (GAO, 2023) reported that sailors in the surface fleet averaged 6.26 hours available for sleep and 5.25 hours of sleep obtained, both below the Navy standard of at least 7.5 hours available for sleep.
text.formatted: The U.S. Government Accountability Office <ref type="bibr">(GAO, 2023)</ref> reported that sailors in the surface fleet averaged 6.26 hours available for sleep and 5.25 hours of sleep obtained, both below the Navy standard of at least 7.5 hours available for sleep.

text.text: The GAO linked inadequate rest to health, safety, and readiness risks and identified heavy workloads and crewing shortfalls as continuing contributors.
A Department of Defense review similarly concluded that sleep deprivation can impair attention, learning, executive function, mood, and operational performance (Department of Defense, 2021b).
These findings support viewing recovery as a readiness variable rather than merely a matter of personal comfort.
The extended 2025-2026 deployment of the USS Abraham Lincoln carrier strike group provides one contemporary illustration.

The Acting Secretary of the Navy stated that the deployment had been extended because of mission requirements and acknowledged that combat operations disrupt normal routines and intensify uncertainty (Department of the Navy, 2026).

Congressional correspondence subsequently described more than 250 days of deployment and more than 200 consecutive days without a port call, while seeking formal information about fatigue, morale, mental health, and crew readiness (King et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Congressional correspondence subsequently described more than 250 days of deployment and more than 200 consecutive days without a port call, while seeking formal information about fatigue, morale, mental health, and crew readiness <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(King et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: The Navy later confirmed eight suicide attempts across the wider strike group during the deployment (Gillibrand & Schneider, 2026).
text.formatted: The Navy later confirmed eight suicide attempts across the wider strike group during the deployment <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Gillibrand & Schneider, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: These reports must not be treated as evidence that deployment duration caused those attempts, nor do they imply that an objective screening instrument would have predicted or prevented them.

They illustrate a broader problem: organizations may have limited systematic information about accumulating strain and recovery before concerns become visible through self-report, clinical presentation, performance failure, or a serious event.

The relevant scientific question is therefore broader than any one ship or deployment: how can military organizations monitor stress-related neurocognitive functioning and recovery early enough to support personnel, training, and readiness without converting normal responses to difficult operations into psychiatric labels?
Answering this question requires a framework that distinguishes exposure from impairment, present performance from compensatory effort, and temporary fatigue from a persistent failure to recover.
The military already uses preventive measurement extensively.
Department of Defense policy requires a Periodic Health Assessment every 12 months.

The standardized process combines self-report, medical-record review, preventive screening, a person-to-person mental-health assessment, and evaluation of medical and deployment readiness (Department of Defense, 2025).
DD Form 3024 formalizes the annual assessment and its role in evaluating health, force readiness, and suitability for deployment (Department of Defense, 2021a).
The same policy links the annual process to required deployment-related health assessments conducted at defined stages (Department of Defense, 2025).
Thus, military readiness is already supported by repeated measurement rather than waiting for a severe physical event to reveal an underlying problem.
Blood-pressure screening offers a useful analogy.
Blood pressure does not diagnose every cardiovascular disorder, and a single elevated reading does not establish that a heart attack will occur.
Its value is that it provides an objective physiological indicator that can reveal risk, prompt repeat measurement, and direct proportionate follow-up before a catastrophic outcome.
The analogy does not imply that mental fitness can be reduced to one biomarker.
It shows why preventive systems combine accessible screening, objective measurement, professional interpretation, and follow-up.
Mental and behavioral health are not absent from military assessment.
Annual mental-health assessment and deployment health screening already provide important opportunities to identify symptoms and facilitate care (Department of Defense, 2025).
text.formatted: Annual mental-health assessment and deployment health screening already provide important opportunities to identify symptoms and facilitate care <ref type="bibr">(Department of Defense, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: The remaining gap concerns objective functional measurement.
Questionnaires depend on recognition, recall, interpretation, and willingness to disclose.
Clinical interviews are appropriately focused on health needs but cannot be repeated continuously across an operational population.
Command observation and performance metrics identify visible behavior, yet acceptable performance can be maintained through increasing compensatory effort.
A service member may therefore perform correctly while requiring progressively greater neurocognitive recruitment, or may recover more slowly after demand without immediately showing an overt error.
Objective brain-based measurement can contribute a complementary layer.
Functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) uses near-infrared light to estimate changes in oxygenated and deoxygenated hemoglobin in superficial cortical tissue.

Portable systems can measure prefrontal hemodynamic responses during structured tasks in settings that are less constrained than conventional neuroimaging laboratories (Ayaz et al., 2012; Pinti et al., 2018). fNIRS does not read thoughts, intentions, memories, political beliefs, or hidden motives.
text.formatted: Portable systems can measure prefrontal hemodynamic responses during structured tasks in settings that are less constrained than conventional neuroimaging laboratories <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Ayaz et al., 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Pinti et al., 2018)</ref>. fNIRS does not read thoughts, intentions, memories, political beliefs, or hidden motives.

text.text: It provides a physiological measure whose meaning depends on the task contrast, behavioral performance, data quality, systemic physiology, and context (Tachtsidis & Scholkmann, 2016; Yücel et al., 2021).
text.formatted: It provides a physiological measure whose meaning depends on the task contrast, behavioral performance, data quality, systemic physiology, and context <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Tachtsidis & Scholkmann, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Yücel et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: The measurement sequence is illustrated in Figure 1.
text.formatted: The measurement sequence is illustrated in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>.

text.text: The purpose is consequently not to replace self-report or professional judgment with a brain signal.
It is to examine how a person functions under controlled demand, what physiological effort accompanies that performance, and how readily the response recovers.
This distinction is central to NPRO-8 MIL.
In practical terms, NPRO-8 MIL asks three operational questions: How much neurocognitive demand is present?
How well does the measured response settle after demand?
Is the pattern accompanied by a change in functional performance?
A service member completes short cognitive tasks while a wearable fNIRS sensor records prefrontal oxygenation.
The analysis combines the physiological response with accuracy and response time, then organizes the result into three pillars.
The technical architecture below explains how those questions are operationalized.
NPRO-8 MIL is the proposed military application of the NPRO-8 Core.
It is a within-person assessment system combining computerized cognitive tasks, behavioral performance, and prefrontal fNIRS.

Rather than relying exclusively on a comparison with population norms, the method examines prespecified contrasts within the examination and evaluates the size of relevant changes in relation to the individual's observed variability (Rotgans, 2026a (Rotgans, , 2026b)).
text.formatted: Rather than relying exclusively on a comparison with population norms, the method examines prespecified contrasts within the examination and evaluates the size of relevant changes in relation to the individual's observed variability <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Rotgans, 2026a</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Rotgans, , 2026b))</ref>.

text.text: This approach is intended to make the assessment sensitive to the pattern of demand, response, and recovery within the person being assessed.
The examination contains five short cognitive task modules derived from established experimental paradigms.

The modules create demands involving sustained engagement and response inhibition, interference control and selective visual attention, cognitive flexibility following a rule change, rule integration and working-memory manipulation, and processing of unexpected or inconsistent feedback.
These functions are central components of executive control and goal-directed behavior (Diamond, 2013).
text.formatted: These functions are central components of executive control and goal-directed behavior <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Diamond, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Behavioral accuracy and response speed are recorded while fNIRS measures associated prefrontal hemodynamic responses.
Within NPRO-8, a NeuroProbe is a prespecified experimental contrast designed to challenge and quantify a neurocognitive function.
It is not an isolated sensor channel, a questionnaire item, or a stand-alone diagnosis.
Each probe combines a controlled task contrast, behavioral performance, and the associated fNIRS response (Rotgans, 2026b).
text.formatted: Each probe combines a controlled task contrast, behavioral performance, and the associated fNIRS response <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Rotgans, 2026b)</ref>.

text.text: The eight core NeuroProbes are summarized below (see Table 1).
text.formatted: The eight core NeuroProbes are summarized below (see Table <ref type="table">1</ref>).

text.text: Table 1 NPRO-8 Core NeuroProbes and Potential Military Relevance NeuroProbe Measured function Illustrative military relevance Sustained task engagement Maintenance of attention and response readiness across repeated trials Vigilance and sustained watchkeeping Response inhibition Suppression of a prepared or habitual response Preventing premature or inappropriate action Interference control Maintenance of the correct response when conflicting information is present Decision control amid competing cues Selective visual-attentional engagement Recruitment of task-relevant visual-attention resources Prioritizing relevant displays or signals Cognitive flexibility Efficient adjustment after a task rule changes Adapting to revised procedures or conditions Rule integration Processing required to invert or transform a learned rule Applying complex or altered instructions Working-memory manipulation Maintenance and use of information across successive trials Holding and updating operational information Mismatch and feedback processing Detection and processing of unexpected or inconsistent feedback Recognizing deviation, surprise, or error signals Note.
Interpretations are screening hypotheses requiring contextual review; they are not diagnoses or automatic fitness determinations.
The NeuroProbe and module-level findings are organized into three higher-order pillars: (1) Stress Load, (2) Recovery Capacity, and (3) Functional Impact.
The pillars are related but intentionally distinct.
Stress Load represents evidence of elevated physiological or neurocognitive demand during baseline and task conditions.

Recovery Capacity represents the extent to which measured activity stabilizes or returns toward baseline following demand, consistent with the broader occupational-health distinction between exposure and recuperation (Sonnentag & Fritz, 2007).
text.formatted: Recovery Capacity represents the extent to which measured activity stabilizes or returns toward baseline following demand, consistent with the broader occupational-health distinction between exposure and recuperation <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Sonnentag & Fritz, 2007)</ref>.

text.text: Functional Impact represents evidence that load or impaired recovery is accompanied by meaningful alteration in task-related neurocognitive functioning (Rotgans, 2026a).
text.formatted: Functional Impact represents evidence that load or impaired recovery is accompanied by meaningful alteration in task-related neurocognitive functioning <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Rotgans, 2026a)</ref>.

text.text: The three-pillar architecture is summarized in Figure 2.
text.formatted: The three-pillar architecture is summarized in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">2</ref>.

text.text: Separating the pillars prevents a single stress score from obscuring different functional profiles.
High load can coexist with preserved performance.
Preserved performance can be achieved through unusually high neural recruitment, suggesting compensation.
Poor recovery can occur before overt performance loss.
Conversely, reduced performance with low activation might reflect fatigue, disengagement, inadequate task understanding, or another explanation rather than excessive stress.
Interpretation therefore requires the combined pattern, behavioral results, data quality, and context.
The principal combinations of behavioral performance and neurocognitive demand are summarized in Table 2.
text.formatted: The principal combinations of behavioral performance and neurocognitive demand are summarized in Table <ref type="table">2</ref>.

text.text: Table 2 Joint Interpretation of Behavioral Performance and Neurocognitive Demand Behavioral performance Neurocognitive demand Provisional interpretation Preserved Stable or reduced Preserved functioning or increasing efficiency Preserved Elevated Possible compensatory effort; performance is maintained at greater physiological cost Reduced Elevated Current demand may exceed available functional capacity Reduced Low or poorly organized Possible fatigue, disengagement, strategy failure, or inadequate task representation Note.
Interpretations are screening hypotheses requiring contextual review; they are not diagnoses or automatic fitness determinations.
Each pillar and the final output are classified Green, Amber, or Red according to prespecified deterministic rules.
Green represents the least concerning classification range, Amber an intermediate or uncertain finding, and Red the most concerning range within the screening system.
These categories are follow-up priorities, not probabilities of illness.

Amber is especially important as a zone in which evidence may be mixed, incomplete, or sensitive to measurement variation and may therefore call for contextual review or repeat assessment rather than a conclusion of impairment (Rotgans, 2026b).
text.formatted: Amber is especially important as a zone in which evidence may be mixed, incomplete, or sensitive to measurement variation and may therefore call for contextual review or repeat assessment rather than a conclusion of impairment <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Rotgans, 2026b)</ref>.

text.text: The framework is designed for repeated measurement.

A single examination describes the measured state under specified conditions; a trajectory can show whether Stress Load is increasing, Recovery Capacity is normalizing, or Functional Impact is changing over time.
Continuous measures, proximity to decision boundaries, and data-quality indicators should remain available rather than reducing longitudinal interpretation to color changes alone.
Illustrative longitudinal pillar trajectories are shown in Figure 3.
text.formatted: Illustrative longitudinal pillar trajectories are shown in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">3</ref>.

text.text: Before a software-based assessment can be evaluated against field outcomes, it must be shown to implement its own analytical specification correctly and to behave predictably when inputs, noise, data availability, and parameters vary.
The internal validation of NPRO-8 Core therefore examined computational validity rather than attempting to establish diagnostic accuracy or prediction of operational outcomes (Rotgans, 2026b).
text.formatted: The internal validation of NPRO-8 Core therefore examined computational validity rather than attempting to establish diagnostic accuracy or prediction of operational outcomes <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Rotgans, 2026b)</ref>.

text.text: A suite of 178 prespecified tests evaluated the input contract, epsilon calculations, minimum evidence requirements, exact decision boundaries, module rules, pillar classifications, and final report aggregation.
All 178 tests passed.
This establishes that the tested software version performed the calculations required by its analytical specification.
Monte Carlo simulation generated synthetic NPRO-8 examinations representing stable profiles and combinations of elevated Stress Load, reduced Recovery Capacity, and Functional Impact.
The complete generated classification was recovered in all 8,000 zero-noise control examinations.
Across the full 32,000 examinations, noise was introduced at four levels.
Detection of generated concerning profiles remained high, while increasing perturbation produced progressively more Amber and Red classifications among generated stable profiles.
This behavior is consistent with a conservative three-pillar roll-up in which the most concerning pillar determines the overall result.
Perfect zero-noise recovery demonstrates internal consistency, not external construct validity.
The generating states were defined using the same conceptual framework implemented by the classifier.
Simulation-based sensitivity and specificity therefore cannot be translated into clinical predictive values or treated as estimates of performance in service members.
A further 50,850 repeated classifications mapped stability at different distances from the decision boundaries and under different levels of noise.
Stability depended strongly on distance from the boundary and on the magnitude of noise relative to epsilon, the within-person variability parameter.
Canonical event ordering produced no changes across 7,200 randomized event-table comparisons.

Missing channels, loss of event markers, and use of the fallback analysis pathway altered some lower-level module or pillar classifications, although the overall result often remained unchanged because another Red pillar continued to determine the final classification.
Parameter-sensitivity analysis showed that the Functional Impact requirement for a Red classification and the adaptive epsilon multiplier were among the most influential design choices.
The analysis did not support changing the production configuration.
This does not establish that the current settings are uniquely optimal; it means that no alternative had sufficient independent evidential support to justify replacing the prespecified settings.

Six opportunistically collected empirical sessions anchored plausible feature ranges and provided realistic examples of signal magnitude, behavioral variability, missing channels, and event-marker structure.
They were not a representative military or occupational sample and cannot support norms, subgroup analyses, or estimates of diagnostic accuracy.
One participant completed a short-interval repeat assessment, offering only a limited single-case indication of stability.

The appropriate conclusion is therefore positive but bounded: NPRO-8 Core has a substantial internally validated computational foundation and is ready for prospective reliability and external-validation studies.
Once the potential value of objective neurocognitive measurement is recognized, an immediate practical limitation becomes apparent.
A military organization cannot routinely fit every member of a carrier crew, brigade, air wing, or installation with an fNIRS device.
Sensor fitting, signal-quality checks, task administration, cleaning, and interpretation require trained personnel and time.
Universal fNIRS assessment would be inefficient and, in many settings, operationally impossible.
The proposed solution is not to abandon objective measurement but to target it.

NPRO-8 MIL should be embedded in a two-tier pathway modeled on preventive screening: a rapid, accessible first tier identifies people or measurement occasions for which the more intensive second tier is likely to be informative (Rotgans, 2026c).
text.formatted: NPRO-8 MIL should be embedded in a two-tier pathway modeled on preventive screening: a rapid, accessible first tier identifies people or measurement occasions for which the more intensive second tier is likely to be informative <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Rotgans, 2026c)</ref>.

text.text: The two tiers describe assessment intensity; they do not replace existing medical, mental-health, safety, or command-support systems.
The military screening and follow-up pathway is summarized in Table 3.
text.formatted: The military screening and follow-up pathway is summarized in Table <ref type="table">3</ref>.

text.text: Tier 1 is a two-to three-minute digital screen combining brief self-report with behavioral measures.
It can be offered at planned intervals rather than only after a complaint or visible performance decline.

Potential measurement points include pre-deployment baseline, scheduled intervals during prolonged deployment, periods following unusually intense operations, return from deployment, and post-deployment recovery.
Green, Amber, and Red outputs would indicate provisional follow-up priorities.

Green would lead to routine monitoring; Amber to contextual review and possible repeat screening; and Red to timely confidential contact and consideration of Tier 2 or conventional professional assessment.
These categories require prospective military calibration.
Self-referral, peer concern, medical referral, and urgent safety pathways must remain available regardless of Tier 1 status so that a brief screen never becomes a barrier to care.
Tier 2 is the approximately ten-minute fNIRS and cognitive assessment, with additional time for explanation, consent, fitting, signal checks, cleaning, and discussion.

Possible indications include Amber or Red Tier 1 results, deterioration across repeated screens, persistent recovery concerns, voluntary request, inclusion in a defined high-exposure cohort, or evaluation of a recovery intervention.
The Tier 2 result should be considered alongside the service member's account, sleep and duty context, medical information when appropriately available, and relevant operational circumstances.
Disagreement between sources should not automatically be resolved in favor of the physiological measure.
Preserved self-reported functioning with elevated neurocognitive demand may reflect compensation, transient context, measurement error, or an emerging vulnerability.
High reported strain with a non-concerning fNIRS profile may reflect demands not reproduced by the assessment, symptoms outside the measured constructs, or limits of the instrument.
Discordance is a reason for inquiry, not for dismissing either source.
An illustrative repeated-measurement and intervention cycle is shown in Figure 4.
text.formatted: An illustrative repeated-measurement and intervention cycle is shown in Figure <ref type="figure">4</ref>.

text.text: Table 3 Military Two-Tier Screening and Follow-Up Pathway Population or trigger Assessment route Resulting action Eligible military personnel Tier 1 broad digital screen Routine monitoring, repeat screening, or confidential review Personnel or measurement occasions meeting prespecified indications Tier 2 targeted NPRO-8 MIL assessment Contextual interpretation, proportionate followup, and longitudinal monitoring Any urgent concern, regardless of screening status Existing clinical and safety pathway Immediate professional assessment and support Note.
Interpretations are screening hypotheses requiring contextual review; they are not diagnoses or automatic fitness determinations.
Note.
The interval and duration shown are illustrative.
Military study schedules should be defined prospectively around deployment phase, operational feasibility, and the research question.
Implementation should proceed through staged validation rather than immediate fleet-wide adoption.
The first phase should establish feasibility, acceptability, completion rates, fNIRS data yield, refusal patterns, time requirements, and logistical burden in a small military sample.
The second should estimate test-retest reliability under stable conditions at the NeuroProbe, module, pillar, and overall levels.
Contextual variables such as sleep, caffeine, medication, time of day, prior duty, pain, and recent exercise should be recorded.
A third phase should follow personnel longitudinally across deployment and recovery.
Measurements should include a pre-deployment baseline, prespecified deployment intervals, high-intensity operational periods when feasible, return, and post-deployment recovery.

Independent comparators might include validated stress and recovery instruments, sleep and duty schedules, psychomotor vigilance, task performance, expert assessment, health-service contact, and prospectively defined functional outcomes.
No single comparator should be assumed to constitute an infallible criterion for stress.

A fourth phase should evaluate incremental validity: whether Tier 2 adds meaningful information beyond Tier 1, standard questionnaires, behavioral performance, sleep measures, and existing readiness processes.
Algorithms and decision thresholds should remain fixed during primary validation and any recalibration should be tested in an independent sample.
Multisite work should examine transportability across services, occupations, sex, age, rank, and relevant demographic groups.
Finally, decision-utility research must determine whether the pathway improves outcomes.

Relevant endpoints include earlier recognition of independently confirmed difficulty, time to appropriate support, recovery monitoring, training modification, and identification of excessively demanding systems or schedules.
Potential harms-including unnecessary referrals, missed concerns, stigma, reduced trust, and career consequences-must be measured alongside potential benefit.
Military hierarchy creates a distinctive consent problem.
Participation may be formally voluntary while a service member reasonably believes that refusal could affect reputation, evaluation, assignment, or career.
The appropriate response is not to deny this pressure but to design procedures that make refusal practically possible and socially safe.

Consent should be managed outside the direct command line; personnel should not have to refuse publicly; and participation or refusal should not be recorded as a performance or behavioral problem (Rotgans Research, 2026).
text.formatted: Consent should be managed outside the direct command line; personnel should not have to refuse publicly; and participation or refusal should not be recorded as a performance or behavioral problem <ref type="bibr">(Rotgans Research, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Individual raw fNIRS data and profiles should not be routinely available to supervisors.
During research and early validation, organizational reports should ordinarily be aggregated, anonymized, or focused on task and system demands.
Individual feedback should be provided privately and only under an agreed protocol.
The data should not be repurposed for promotion, selection, discipline, or deployability decisions without a separate evidentiary and ethical basis, appropriate authorization, and transparent policy.

Data governance should specify who controls the raw data, how identifiers are separated, who may access the code key, retention periods, withdrawal procedures, cybersecurity controls, and conditions for secondary use.
Data minimization is especially important because neurophysiological data may be perceived as more revealing than their actual scientific content.
fNIRS measures hemodynamic changes in superficial cortical areas during specified tasks.
It cannot reveal thoughts, memories, loyalties, beliefs, or concealed intentions.
NPRO-8 MIL is not intended to diagnose posttraumatic stress disorder, depression, anxiety, burnout, attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, or any other medical or psychiatric condition.
Nor should it function autonomously as a psychological selection or fitnessfor-duty instrument.
Objective measurement may also offer ethical benefits.
Observable behavior does not always show why a task is difficult.
Two personnel can produce the same correct response while one does so efficiently and the other through unusually high neurocognitive recruitment.
A system that makes this difference visible may support fairer training, more appropriate recovery, safer watch schedules, better interfaces, and improved automation.
The ethical objective is therefore not to determine whether a person is suitable, but to understand where demands exceed current resources and how training, systems, or support can be improved.
NPRO-8 MIL addresses a specific gap between broad mental-health screening and detailed laboratory neurocognitive assessment.
Its central proposition is that military mental fitness should be examined as a dynamic pattern of load, recovery, and functioning rather than inferred from symptoms or observable performance alone.

This proposition is consistent with models of allostatic load, effort-recovery, work ability, and executive function, all of which distinguish exposure from adaptation and adaptation from functional consequence (McEwen, 1998; Meijman & Mulder, 1998; Rotgans, 2026a).
text.formatted: This proposition is consistent with models of allostatic load, effort-recovery, work ability, and executive function, all of which distinguish exposure from adaptation and adaptation from functional consequence <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(McEwen, 1998;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Meijman & Mulder, 1998;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Rotgans, 2026a)</ref>.

text.text: The framework is especially relevant to prolonged deployment because performance can be preserved for some time through compensation.
A service member may continue to meet standards while the physiological effort required increases and recovery becomes less complete.
Conversely, a temporary high-load response during a difficult task may be appropriate and should not be pathologized.
By separating Stress Load, Recovery Capacity, and Functional Impact, NPRO-8 MIL creates a structure for distinguishing these patterns.
The internal-validation evidence is an important strength.

The NPRO-8 Core is not entering military research as an untested scoring idea: its programmed rules, known-state recovery, robustness, event ordering, and parameter dependence have been examined systematically.
At the same time, computational correctness is not the same as field validity.
The Monte Carlo evidence cannot establish that a Red profile corresponds to actual operational impairment or that a Green profile predicts safety.
Those questions require prospective military data and independent outcomes.
The two-tier architecture makes the proposal operationally plausible.
Broad screening supplies reach; targeted fNIRS supplies depth.
Repeated measurements allow trajectory-based interpretation rather than reliance on a single state.
Importantly, the pathway should augment rather than displace existing medical and behavioral-health systems.
Urgent concerns require conventional safety and clinical responses irrespective of a screening result.
The eight NeuroProbes should be regarded as the validated core architecture.

Additional military-specific probes could later address divided attention, threat monitoring, vigilance decrement, spatial working memory, prospective memory, multitasking, automation monitoring, alarm prioritization, team coordination, or recovery after sustained watchkeeping.
Each extension would require a defined task contrast, internal verification, reliability analysis, and independent empirical validation before inclusion in operational reporting.
NPRO-8 MIL therefore offers a research and decision-support framework for objective assessment of stress-related neurocognitive functioning.

Its appropriate next step is a carefully governed prospective military program establishing feasibility, test-retest reliability, external validity, sensitivity to deployment and recovery, incremental value, and decision utility.
If those stages are successful, the framework could complement established readiness systems by making the neurocognitive cost of sustained performance and the capacity for recovery more visible.
Military organizations measure physical and medical readiness repeatedly because important risks cannot be managed solely by waiting for symptoms or failure.
Stress-related neurocognitive functioning presents an analogous, although more complex, measurement challenge.
NPRO-8 MIL provides a structured approach combining behavioral performance and task-evoked fNIRS across eight NeuroProbes and three pillars: Stress Load, Recovery Capacity, and Functional Impact.
The underlying NPRO-8 Core has demonstrated computational coherence through deterministic testing, Monte Carlo known-state simulation, robustness analysis, and parameter-sensitivity testing.
This foundation supports progression to prospective military research but does not substitute for it.
A two-tier pathway-broad digital screening followed by targeted objective assessment-offers a feasible model for scale.
Its legitimacy depends on rigorous validation and equally rigorous governance protecting voluntariness, privacy, purpose limitation, and human review.
Used within those boundaries, NPRO-8 MIL may help military organizations identify accumulating strain, incomplete recovery, and emerging functional vulnerability earlier and more objectively.
